k-1.x_notes: Ten concrete, play-based problems with drawn counters; the mathematics checks out (P4 vs greedy Ben: 3,4,6,7; P7: 1st, 2nd, 2nd; P8 two-pile pairs correct). Good sequence: {1,2}, then {1,2,3} and {1,3} across 1-12, then 20 counters and two piles, so the band doesn't run out early. Clean format. Weaknesses: P1 uses piles 2-5, which has only one second-player pile (3). P9 and P10 share one page as small side-by-side dot grids with no example of the ringing convention, which kindergartners will need to have shown to them. P10 is just enumeration and never connects back to who wins.
k-1.y_notes: The problems are almost the same as X's and just as correct. P1 uses piles 3-6, so two second-player piles (3, 6) appear and hint at the pattern. P4 says who plays Ben ('Your partner plays Ben'). P8 restates that whoever takes the very last counter wins, which matters once there are two piles. P9 and P10 each get a full-page board, and P9 has one game already ringed (2+2) to show how to record, which helps K-1 children. P10 adds a purposeful task: star each game the first player wins (4 of the 8), which ties the counting back to the game. Minor: one extra page, and the worked ring gives away one of the five games.
k-1.reason: Same core problems; Y's model ring, larger enumeration boards and the 'star the first-player wins' task make the last two problems easier to start and more meaningful for young children, and P1 shows a better spread of piles.

grades-2-3.x_notes: A strong, correct sequence: P1 {1,2} piles; P2 four plans to test (Mia wins, Leo loses, Ana wins, Sam always loses); P3 {1,3,4} 1-20 (losing piles 2,7,9,14,16); P4 large piles 25/30/37/50 (1st, 2nd, 2nd, 1st); P5 Kai/Theo lose, Zoe wins; P6 {1,2,4} vs {1,2} (Jon is wrong, both give multiples of 3); P7 two piles with a mirror argument. Weaknesses: P6 gives a blank two-row table without saying what to write in the cells, and has no space for the answer to 'Is Jon right?'. P5 never asks why Zoe's winning plan can't lose, which is the band's emphasis (answer every reply). 'I start with 8 counters' can be misread as the player holding the counters.
grades-2-3.y_notes: Same problems and answers as X, all correct. Y fixes X's gaps. P5 asks children to explain why a winning plan can never lose (Zoe), which is exactly the outline's 'test against every reply'. P6 says to shade the second-player piles on two number strips, asks for an explanation that holds beyond 15, and gives a large answer box. 'The pile has 8 counters' is clearer. P7 gets its own page with a big workspace. Minor: one more 'explain' request and one more page.
grades-2-3.reason: The content is otherwise identical; Y's P6 is clearer to act on and has room to answer, and its P5 asks for the justification that the band's emphasis calls for. X would need small edits to fix both.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Rich and correct. P3's seven rules pair up ({1,2}={1,2,4}, {1,3}={1,3,5}, {1,4}={1,4,6}). The greedy-Kai problem is well posed and precisely worded (mistakes at 5,8,10,12,...; greedy is safe only for {1,3} and {1,3,5}). The P5 inverse problems include a genuine construction ({1,2,6} for 3,7,10,...) and an impossible case (3,5,8,...). The {1,6,9} problem has a real pre-period (periodic from 10) plus the pigeonhole question. P8's Grundy labels give correct pairs (11/13 losing, 12/18 winning). Weaknesses: the first two P5 lists (4,8,12 and 2,5,7,10) can be read straight off P3, so half of P5 is lookup. P7's {1,3,4} grid is fill-in only, with no question and no answer box. P8 introduces the labels without asking how they connect to the pair grids, so the purpose of the mex rule is left implicit. P4 doesn't ask for any explanation. The P3 strips have small cells.
grades-4-5.y_notes: The same strong core, all correct, in a better order and with purposeful changes. P5's lists 5,10,15 ({1,2,3,4}) and 2,8,10,16,18 ({1,4,5}, a real construction) take the place of X's lookup cases, alongside {1,2,6} and the impossible list. P4 asks children to explain one rule where greedy is never a mistake (parity). The periodicity problem comes earlier, so the two-pile grids lead straight into the labels. P8 asks for losing pairs with unequal piles (0/2/7, 1/3/8, 4/6), and P9 asks how the labels predict the grid's losing pairs. That makes the Sprague-Grundy idea discoverable from the children's own data rather than an unexplained definition. P3 strips are more spacious. Minor: 'a mistake' is slightly less precise than X's wording; one more page; slightly more 'explain' prompts.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are mathematically sound, but Y's inverse problem has no trivial lookups, every problem ends in a real question, and the grid-then-labels sequence with an explicit link lets 4-5th graders discover why the labels work instead of just computing them.

overall.reason: The two packets share nearly all their problems and both are correct and well paced, but Y is consistently a little better in every band: a model and a purpose for the K-1 enumeration, clearer instructions and room to justify in grades 2-3, and a richer, better-sequenced path to the labels in grades 4-5. None of X's weaknesses would cause real trouble in class, but Y needs less of the organizer's fifteen minutes of editing.
